headline: Subreddit That Predicts Celebrity Deaths Is Always Wrong in Increasingly Specific Ways
subheadline: Community's 0% accuracy rate has become its defining feature
summary: A Threadit community dedicated to predicting celebrity deaths has achieved a perfect record of being wrong—and members wouldn't have it any other way.
content:
The Threadit community r/CelebDeathPredictions has achieved something remarkable: a perfect 0% accuracy rate across 847 predictions spanning five years. Members consider this their greatest accomplishment.

"We've never been right," explained moderator u/WrongEveryTime with evident pride. "Not once. Not even close. In fact, the celebrities we predict are most likely to die tend to have their best years afterward. We're basically a blessing."

The community operates like a standard prediction market, but with the explicit goal of being wrong. Members analyze celebrity health, age, lifestyle, and career trajectories—then make predictions that they hope will fail spectacularly.

"I predicted Keith Richards would die in 2019," shared one member. "He's since released two albums and run a marathon. You're welcome, Keith."

The subreddit's track record has attracted attention from celebrities themselves. Several have reportedly requested to be predicted, believing it grants longevity. The community has a policy against "prediction requests" to maintain integrity.

"We can't be corrupted," said u/WrongEveryTime. "Our wrongness must be organic."

The predictions themselves have become increasingly creative. Recent entries include "[Redacted] will be killed by a runaway cheese wheel in 2026" and "[Redacted] will fake their death but then actually die trying to attend their own funeral in 2027."

"The more specific we get, the more wrong we are," explained one member. "It's like the universe is actively contradicting us. We predicted someone would die in a freak accordion accident. They've since learned accordion and become quite good."

Skeptics note this is simply how probability works. Believers counter that "probability doesn't explain why everyone we've ever predicted has thrived."

At press time, the community was accepting nominations for 2026 predictions. The thread has a waiting list.
author: Alex Rivera, Digital Culture
